notes:
Now I will compose the verse-by-verse notes based on the sources I have read. I'll note the tradition where possible, though many traditional readings overlap across traditions. I have material from Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist), Ellicott (older Anglican), Precept Austin (Evangelical), Ligonier (Reformed), Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, and Bible.org.

---

# Nehemiah 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

**Overview of the Chapter.** The chapter describes the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, moving counterclockwise from the Sheep Gate (northeast corner) around the city back to the Sheep Gate. It names about 44 groups of workers. The Hebrew word for "repaired" is *chazaq* (strengthen, make strong), used 35 times in this chapter alone (Enduring Word). Commentators agree the chapter is not merely a list of names — it teaches the importance of cooperation, godly leadership, and whole-community involvement in God's work.

---

## v. 1: Eliashib, Sheep Gate, Tower of the Hundred, Tower of Hananel

- **Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests.** Eliashib was the grandson of Jeshua (or Joshua), the high priest who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; Neh 12:10). By rising first, he set a powerful example for both priests and people (Gill). Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that the high priest "acted as a godly leader should — he was out in front of the work, leading by example" rather than being "too 'spiritual' for the hard work." More than 50 others followed his example.
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

- **The Sheep Gate.** So named because sheep for sacrifice were brought through it. Near it was the pool of Bethesda (John 5:2), where sheep were washed before sacrifice. It was in the priests' quarter near the temple. Guzik says Nehemiah started here because it represented "making sure the important part of the temple worship, sacrifice for the sins of the people, is taken care of first" (Precept Austin, citing Brian Bell). Gill says it was "to the south of the city," though most modern reconstructions place it on the northeast.
  - Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-3-commentary
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

- **They dedicated/consecrated it.** This was a separate consecration from the general dedication of the whole wall (Neh 12:27–43). By consecrating the first-fruits of the building, they dedicated the entire project to God. Guzik: "These city gates were made especially for God… a way for them to say, 'All of this work belongs to You, LORD.'" Gill adds that they "prayed for a blessing on it, and in it on the whole work undertaken."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Precept Austin (Utley): https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-3-commentary

- **Tower of the Hundred (Hammeah) and Tower of Hananel.** These were at the northeast corner of the wall. "Meah" means "hundred," possibly referring to an elite military unit of a hundred men or its height (100 cubits). The Tower of Hananel is mentioned in Jeremiah 31:38 as part of restoration prophecy. These towers stood close together and were "the most vulnerable to attack" since they were not protected by valleys (Precept Austin, Brian Bell).
  - Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-3-commentary
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 2: Men of Jericho; Zaccur son of Imri

- **The men of Jericho.** Ellicott notes they built "at the point… opposite their own city" (Jericho lies northeast of Jerusalem). Gill says they began where the priests ended. Their participation shows that people from outlying towns, not just Jerusalem residents, joined the work.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

- **Zaccur son of Imri.** Probably the chief or leader of the men of Jericho (Gill). Little else is known about him.
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 3: Fish Gate; sons of Hassenaah

- **The Fish Gate.** Through which fish entered from the Jordan, Galilee, and the Mediterranean coast. Near it was the fish market. It was on the north wall. Gill places it westward "towards the Mediterranean sea, Tyre, and Joppa." Ellicott: "Through which fish entered from the Jordan and Galilee."
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

- **The sons of Hassenaah.** Unusually, their individual names are not given (Ellicott notes this is "contrary to custom"). They laid beams, doors, bolts, and bars — meaning they completely finished the gate.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 4: Meremoth, Meshullam, Zadok

- **Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz.** Also mentioned in Ezra 8:33 as a priest who weighed the temple silver and gold. He does *two* sections — here and again in v. 21, showing his zeal (Ellicott; Gill). The word "repaired" (*chazaq*) means "strengthened" — this section of wall was not wholly destroyed but needed strengthening.
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

- **Meshullam son of Berechiah.** He appears again in v. 30 working in front of his own quarters (a single room). Guzik notes that this man had only "one small room, yet he was devoted to God and to the work." His name means "devoted" or "surrendered."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/

- **Zadok son of Baana.** Nothing further known about him (Gill).

---

## v. 5: The Tekoites and their nobles

- **The Tekoites made repairs.** Tekoa was a town in Judah, home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). The ordinary people worked willingly. Ellicott notes that the men of Tekoa were "not mentioned among Zerubbabel's Returned," making their participation remarkable.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

- **But their nobles did not put their shoulders to the work.** Literally in Hebrew, "did not bring their necks to the work" — a picture of refusing to submit, like oxen refusing the yoke (Gill; Enduring Word). Guzik calls this "the solitary instance of internal opposition to the building" and says these nobles "stand in infamy as the only people mentioned in this chapter who did not join in." Ellicott says they furnish "the solitary instance of internal opposition." The work is called "the work of their Lord" — indicating the building was seen as service to God Himself. Notably, the common Tekoites did *double duty* (v. 27 also), compensating for their nobles' failure.
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 6: The Jeshanah Gate (Old Gate)

- **The Jeshanah Gate.** The KJV calls it the "Old Gate." Ellicott says it is "not mentioned elsewhere: probably that of Damascus," though some conjecture it means "the gate of the old wall" (distinguished from the "Broad Wall"). Gill says it "led to the old city Salem." It was on the north or northwest section.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

- **Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah.** They laid beams, doors, bolts, and bars — completing the gate fully. These are not the same Meshullam as v. 4.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 7: Melatiah the Gibeonite, Jadon the Meronothite; authority of the governor

- **Melatiah and Jadon.** From Gibeon and Mizpah (both in Benjamin — Joshua 18:25). Some of these builders "were not Israelites by birth" (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary). They worked "under the authority of the governor of the region west of the Euphrates" — i.e., they answered to the Persian-appointed governor (the *pechah*). Ellicott says this refers to "the seat of the pechah of the whole district this side the Euphrates: his residence when he came to Jerusalem." Aben Ezra (cited by Gill) suggests "the throne" (*cissē*) might be a man's name — "Cisse" — who was the governor.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-3.html

---

## v. 8: Uzziel the goldsmith, Hananiah the perfumer; the Broad Wall

- **Uzziel (goldsmith) and Hananiah (perfumer/apothecary).** Neither was a professional builder. Guzik: "These were men of different professions, not professional builders. They were not trained for this kind of work. It would have seemed they had an easy excuse to not do anything, but they jumped in and did the work." This illustrates that "the most important ability in the work of the LORD is availability." Yamauchi (cited by Guzik) noted that no expert builders are listed — only priests, goldsmiths, perfume-makers, and women.
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/

- **They fortified Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall.** The Broad Wall was more than 20 feet (6 meters) wide and can still be seen in Jerusalem today. Guzik says, "Critics had denied the accuracy of Bible history like this, but the archaeologist's shovel constantly confirms the truth of the Bible." Ellicott, however, suggests the Hebrew means they "left" Jerusalem untouched as far as the Broad Wall, since that portion needed no restoration (it had been built so strongly by Uzziah that it still stood — cf. 2 Chronicles 25:23).
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 9: Rephaiah son of Hur

- **Rephaiah, ruler of a half-district of Jerusalem.** Jerusalem was divided into two half-districts, one under a governor from Judah (this man, likely) and another from Benjamin (v. 12 — Shallum). This shows that even rulers got their hands dirty. Guzik: "Here was another leader who knew real leadership is getting down and doing it — being a servant, instead of expecting others to do it for you."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 10: Jedaiah (opposite his house); Hattush

- **Jedaiah made repairs across from his house.** This is one of several instances where people worked on the wall directly in front of their own home. Guzik notes his name means "he who calls unto God" — suggesting "our homes must be places of prayer." Working by one's own house increased motivation (protection of family), saved travel time, and ensured quality work (Precept Austin).
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-3-commentary

- **Hattush son of Hashabneiah.** Unknown beyond this verse (Gill).

---

## v. 11: Malchijah, Hasshub; Tower of the Ovens

- **Malchijah son of Harim.** This man appears in Ezra 10:31 as one who had married a pagan wife and was confronted by Ezra. Guzik: "That was many years before this, so Malchijah got things right with God and now, years later, he served Him. A believer should never let a past failure get in the way of serving God."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/

- **Hasshub son of Pahath-moab.** His father was head of a family that returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:6). The "other section" (second piece) refers to a second measured portion of wall.

- **The Tower of the Ovens** (or Tower of the Furnaces). Near it were furnaces for baking bread or bricks (Gill).

---

## v. 12: Shallum and his daughters

- **Shallum, ruler of the other half-district of Jerusalem.** He governed the Benjamin side of Jerusalem (see note on v. 9).

- **He and his daughters made repairs.** Ellicott says some think "daughters" refers to the villages of the district — but he calls this "needless," noting that "the women of Jerusalem might do voluntarily what as females they were not pressed to do." Gill says the daughters "were rich widows or heiresses, and employed men to build at their own expense." Guzik simply says, "Everyone who could help did help." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary cites this as evidence that God's work involves "men and women, filling every place of service."
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-3.html

---

## v. 13: The Valley Gate; thousand cubits to the Dung Gate

- **The Valley Gate.** On the southwest corner of the wall, overlooking the Valley of Hinnom (Garner-Howes). Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah (a city in Judah, Joshua 15:34) rebuilt it.

- **A thousand cubits of the wall.** About 1,500 feet (roughly 450 metres). Ellicott notes this is a round number and this stretch "had probably suffered less damage, and therefore needed less repairing." The word implies "strengthening" rather than building from scratch.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 14: The Dung Gate

- **The Dung Gate** (Refuse Gate). On the south wall. Used to remove garbage and offal from the city and temple (Garner-Howes). Malchijah son of Rechab — not necessarily a Rechabite, despite the name (Ellicott) — ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem (between Tekoa and Jerusalem, Jeremiah 6:1) rebuilt it completely.

---

## v. 15: The Fountain Gate; Pool of Shelah (Siloam); stairs from City of David

- **The Fountain Gate.** On the southeast corner, looking out to the juncture of the Hinnom and Kidron valleys (Garner-Howes). Shallun (or Shallum) son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, "covered" (roofed) it — the only gate specifically said to be roofed, perhaps because of the fountain nearby (Gill).

- **The Pool of Shelah (Siloah/Siloam).** Called "the king's pool" elsewhere; received water through a long subterranean conduit from the Gihon spring, and supplied the king's gardens (Ellicott). Spurgeon preached a sermon from the phrase "the king's garden," speaking of six gardens of the King: Eden, Gethsemane, the garden tomb, the human heart, the church, and paradise in heaven (Enduring Word).
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

- **The stairs that descend from the City of David.** Down the steep sides of Ophel; traces of these stairs are thought still to remain (Ellicott).

---

## v. 16: Nehemiah son of Azbuk; tombs of David; the artificial pool; House of the Mighty

- **Nehemiah son of Azbuk.** Not the governor Nehemiah, but a different man with the same name. He was ruler of a half-district of Beth-zur, a fortified town in Judah (Joshua 15:58).

- **Opposite the tombs of David.** Excavated on the western side of the Temple — "never yet traced," says Ellicott.

- **The artificial pool.** Possibly the reservoir of Hezekiah (Isaiah 22:11; 2 Kings 20:20). The "House of the Mighty" may have been the barracks of David's elite troops (1 Chronicles 11:10).
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 17–18: Levites; Hashabiah and Binnui of Keilah

- **The Levites made repairs under Rehum son of Bani.** The circuit is now approaching the temple area. Levites as a body worked under Rehum (Ellicott).

- **Hashabiah, ruler of a half-district of Keilah** (a city in Judah, Joshua 15:44) made repairs "for his district" — i.e., with men under his jurisdiction or at the expense of his half.

- **Binnui (Bavai) son of Henadad, ruler of the other half-district of Keilah.** Together the two half-district rulers covered the whole of Keilah's obligation.

---

## v. 19: Ezer son of Jeshua; Ascent to the Armory

- **Ezer, ruler of Mizpah.** Either the other half of Mizpah (see v. 15) or a different Mizpah.

- **Opposite the Ascent to the Armory, near the angle in the wall.** Ellicott translates "the armoury of the corner" — the northwest corner of the "City of David" with its special wall. The armory was where weapons were stored, perhaps "the same with the tower of David" alluded to in Song of Solomon 4:4 (Gill).
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 20: Baruch son of Zabbai

- **Baruch diligently repaired.** The Hebrew word rendered "diligently" (or "earnestly," KJV) carries the sense of doing something "in anger" or with burning zeal. Gill: "being angry with himself or others that there was any backwardness shown to the work; and therefore, with all haste and eagerness imaginable, attended to it." Ellicott says, "The reason of this man's emulation in building near the high priest's house does not appear." Precept Austin (Steven Cole) notes that "it was only said of Baruch that he carefully (or zealously) repaired his section" — setting him apart as exemplary. Ligonier (Reformed) notes that Nehemiah as a leader both "noted who did the work and who didn't" and gave recognition where due.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-3-commentary
  - Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/work-on-wall-begins

- **From the angle to the doorway of the house of Eliashib the high priest.** This connects Baruch's section to the high priest's residence.

---

## v. 21: Meremoth (second section)

- **Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired another section.** This is his *second* assignment (see v. 4). Having finished his first section, he volunteered for more — "from the doorway of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house." The high priest's house was large, and the section along its length was considerable (Gill). Meremoth's double duty exemplifies going "above and beyond."
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 22: The priests from the surrounding area

- **The priests, the men of the plain.** Ellicott understands this as "priests dwelling in the Jordan valley, the 'Kikkar' of Scripture" — i.e., the plain around Jericho. These were priests who lived outside Jerusalem but came to help. Alternatively, Gill thinks it means "the plain about Jerusalem."
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 23: Benjamin and Hasshub; Azariah

- **Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs in front of their house.** Guzik notes the name "Benjamin" means "son of my right hand" — speaking of a protector; "our homes must be places of protection and peace."

- **Azariah son of Maaseiah made repairs beside his house.** Working near one's own home ensured personal investment and good workmanship (Precept Austin).
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-3-commentary

---

## v. 24: Binnui son of Henadad

- **Binnui repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the angle and the corner.** This corner was the "north-eastern angle of the 'City of David'" (Ellicott).
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 25: Palal; the tower jutting from the upper palace; Pedaiah

- **Palal son of Uzai** worked opposite the angle and the tower projecting from the king's upper palace near the courtyard of the guard. This was the "high tower outlying from the king's palace" (Ellicott). The palace had its own prison; the "prison-gate" is mentioned in Nehemiah 12:39 (Ellicott). We read in Jeremiah of "the court of the prison" being in or near the king's house (Jeremiah 32:2; Gill).

---

## v. 26: The temple servants (Nethinim) on Ophel

- **The temple servants living on the hill of Ophel.** Ophel was the long rounded spur running south of the Temple. The Nethinim (temple servants assigned to assist the Levites) dwelt there, separated from others (Ellicott). Their work included fetching water for the temple, so their location near the Water Gate was fitting (Gill). They repaired "opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the tower that juts out." Ellicott notes that nothing is said of their part in the general labour apart from this location-based work.
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 27: The Tekoites (second section)

- **The Tekoites repaired another section.** This is the second section the Tekoites undertook (see v. 5). Their nobles had refused to work, but the common people of Tekoa did *double duty*. Guzik: "They weren't going to let the bad example of their nobles… keep them from working above and beyond the call of duty." Ellicott notes they worked "from a point opposite the great tower that juts out to the wall of Ophel."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 28: Above the Horse Gate

- **The Horse Gate.** Between the Temple and the palace. So called either because near it were stables for horses, or horses were led through it to be watered at the Kidron brook (Gill). Josephus mentions a "horse tower" nearby. "Above" the Horse Gate means the section just north of it. Each of the priests made repairs in front of his own house — showing there was a row of priests' houses along this stretch.
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-3.html

---

## v. 29: Zadok son of Immer; Shemaiah, keeper of the East Gate

- **Zadok son of Immer** made repairs opposite his house. His name means "justice" — Guzik says, "Our homes must be places of justice and integrity."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/

- **Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, the guard of the East Gate.** The East Gate gave access to the temple area. Gill says Shemaiah was "keeper of the east gate… of the temple; for the gates of the city having been burnt so long, it cannot be thought there should be a keeper of any of them." He pitched in at the Horse Gate section rather than his own — a display of unselfishness (Guzik). Ellicott notes the name appears in 1 Chronicles 3:22 as a descendant of David.
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## v. 30: Hananiah, Hanun (sixth son of Zalaph), Meshullam

- **Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph.** Hanun is specifically identified as the *sixth* son, which Gill says is "observed to his great commendation" — the youngest of six sons yet he laboured.
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

- **Meshullam son of Berechiah** (also in v. 4) repaired opposite his own quarters. The Hebrew word for "quarters" means "chamber" — a single room. Guzik: "Meshullam had only one small room, yet he was devoted to God and to the work of rebuilding the walls. It is better to be devoted to God in one small room than to have a mansion and have a heart cold towards God." His name means "devoted."
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/

---

## v. 31–32: The Inspection (Miphkad) Gate; finishing at the Sheep Gate

- **Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths.** Not a professional builder but a tradesman who made himself available. He repaired as far as the house of the temple servants and the merchants, opposite the Inspection Gate (Miphkad Gate — perhaps meaning "muster" or "assembly" gate). Some think it was where the Sanhedrin sat and tried cases (Gill). Ellicott suggests a connection between the merchants who sold doves and other items for worship and the Nethinim, near whose house they brought them.

- **Between the upper room above the corner and the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and the merchants made repairs.** This completed the circuit — the wall returned to where it began (v. 1). Guzik notes, "It appears that the 'goldsmiths and the merchants' undertook the small space necessary to complete the circuit." The entire wall was rebuilt in 52 days (Neh 6:15).
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/3.htm
  - Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/
  - Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/3.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives

### Reformed (Ligonier.org)

Ligonier emphasises the *unity* of God's people under one mission regardless of background. "When God's people are united under one mission regardless of their background, much good can be accomplished." The rebuilding is seen as an act of reformation — restoring proper worship and community — and Nehemiah's faith and strength of character in the face of enemies (Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem) are highlighted. The application moves to Ephesians 4:1–16: the church united in truth and love, not tossed by cunning and craftiness.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/work-on-wall-begins

### Baptist (Garner-Howes)

The Baptist commentary stresses that "it takes all God's people, of all walks of life, men and women, filling every place of service, to accomplish the greatest good in the cause of Christ (2 Corinthians 6:1)." It draws four lessons: (1) the Lord expects cooperation; (2) family, community, and occupational groups should all be interested in the work of Christ; (3) access and exit in the Lord's churches should be strong and well guarded; (4) no area of worship should be neglected.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-3.html

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

Guzik (generally aligned with Calvary Chapel's charismatic-evangelical tradition) sees the chapter as pointing to Jesus at every turn: Jesus the builder (greater than Nehemiah), Jesus the servant High Priest (greater than Eliashib), and Jesus the Messiah whose birth was made possible by the security the wall provided. He also emphasises consecration (setting apart for God), the spiritual meaning of names, and the principle that "availability matters far more than credentials."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-3/

### Evangelical (Bible.org / Precept Austin)

Steven Cole (Bible.org) explicitly *rejects* allegorising the gates (Sheep Gate = Christ the Good Shepherd, Fish Gate = fishers of men, etc.), calling it not the meaning of the text. Instead, the chapter is "to show us the importance of working together to accomplish God's purpose." The three elements needed: common vision, dedicated leaders, and willing workers. Cole warns against "spectators" in the church, likening the 80/20 principle to a football game where 30,000 who need exercise watch 22 who need rest.
